job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Carlos Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior analyst in the finance planning team at Dunmore Freight, a logistics company outside Birmingham. I build the monthly cost reports, update forecasts and answer questions from the depot managers about why their fuel numbers are off. I probably have an AI assistant open for half of it. I share a terraced house with three people from my course, and I do a bit of freelance spreadsheet work in the evenings because my student loan is huge and my savings are close to zero.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say fine, it's a handy tool and not magic, and my team is already faster because of it. To friends I'd say people who sneer at it are mostly the ones who've never learned to use it well. Online I'd probably share a tip or two and not much opinion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't scare me much. I'm already using it, so if it stays a helper then I'm the guy who's good at it, and that's a small edge. What does bother me is the loan and the rent, because my pay is low and the number of finance jobs near here is tiny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building my own little library of prompts and spreadsheet templates, and I'd try to turn them into something the whole team uses. I'd keep the freelance jobs, about 300 a month, and put 100 into savings. I'd also apply for an analyst role at one of the bigger firms in the city, to see what I'd be worth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, actually, with a little worry on the side. I feel like I'm on a long bike ride where the hills are the money, not the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use an AI assistant half the day. What happens to that in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the weekly variance commentary, the part where you explain why costs moved. The assistant drafts it, I fix it. It saves me about three hours, and I'd use that time to talk to the depot managers, which is where I learn the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the freelance work look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small stuff: a bakery's stock sheets, a landlord's rent tracker, a charity's budget. I charge cheap, around 25 an hour, and get about 10 hours a month. It's not much but it's cash, and it also shows me how other businesses run.

say: I'd say it's a **handy tool**, not magic, and my team is already faster.
I'd say people who sneer at it have rarely learned to use it **well**.
think: If it stays a helper, I'm the guy who's **good at it**, and that's a small edge.
My real worry is the **loan** and rent on low pay with few jobs nearby.
do: Build a shared library of **prompts** and spreadsheet templates for my team.
Keep the freelance jobs, about **300** a month, and save 100.
Apply to a bigger firm in the city to see what I'm **worth**.
feel: **Good**, with a little worry, like a bike ride where the hills are money.
S0.quote: I feel like I'm on a long bike ride where the hills are the money, not the work.
fieldNote: He sees AI as his **edge**, so the plateau doesn't scare him; the debt does.
He's already earning small side money and learning how other businesses run.
Testing his market value by applying elsewhere is typical of his curious style.

steps.text: Build a shared prompt and template library for the team
Keep freelance spreadsheet work and save 100 a month
Apply for an analyst role at a bigger city firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big deal and people should get on with it, rather than argue about it. At work I'd offer to run a short session on how I use the assistant. I'd also say loudly that companies shouldn't cut people just because a tool is cheaper this quarter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the junior analyst job is about to be two jobs fewer. If I can do the work of three people with a good assistant, the company will notice, and the question is whether they'll keep me or the one who doesn't use it. I think I'm in the better pile, but my manager, Priya, can't promise anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push to be the one who automates our monthly reporting end to end, so I'm tied to the thing that makes the savings, not the thing that gets replaced. I'd start learning SQL and how to connect the reports to the company's data. I'd also expand freelance, with a small package for small firms, 400 a month for set-up and upkeep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buzzing and a bit sick at once. It's exciting to be early, and then I remember I owe the bank a ridiculous amount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your own job is all about forecasting and reports. How hard does that get hit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gets hit hard. The routine reports are exactly what the assistant does, so the team will do the same work with fewer people. What survives is the explaining, so I'd move toward the part where I stand in front of depot managers and tell them what to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the freelance side if your day job shrinks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put more hours in and try to land three or four regular clients, maybe a chain of small cafes. I'd use my own assistant to cut each job to a few hours. If the day job went, the freelance could cover rent but not the loan.

say: I'd say it's a **big deal** and we should get on with it, not argue.
I'd offer a short **session** at work on how I use the assistant.
think: The junior analyst job is about to be **two jobs fewer**, and I think I'm in the better pile.
My manager, Priya (my boss), **can't promise** anything.
do: Automate our monthly **reporting** end to end so I'm tied to the savings.
Learn **SQL** to connect reports to the company's data.
Grow freelance with a **set-up** package for small firms, about 400 a month.
feel: **Buzzing** and a bit sick at once, because I owe the bank so much.
S1.quote: I'd push to be the one who automates our monthly reporting end to end, so I'm tied to the thing that makes the savings, not the thing that gets replaced.
fieldNote: He wants to be on the **automating** side of the change, not the replaced side.
Excitement and nausea sit together; the loan is what undercuts his confidence.
He doesn't over-trust his manager and builds his own freelance fallback.

steps.text: Automate the monthly cost reporting end to end
Learn SQL and connect reports to company data
Sell a 400-a-month reporting set-up to small firms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should stop pretending it's a normal restructure and be honest that the rules will have to change. I'd say governments need to get ready, with income support and a say for ordinary workers. I'd post about it, loudly. I'd also say the companies making the savings should pay for the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be a lucky one for a year or so and then not. I'm good with the tools, but AGI means the tools get better than me. The finance planning job is thinking work, so it's among the first to go, and using AI every day isn't a moat when the AI can do my job without me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd immediately cut costs to the bone and try to bank 500 a month by working even more freelance hours. I'd look for work that depends on trust and presence, maybe running money for a local credit union, or working with a startup that sells to the people who lose jobs. I'd talk to my uncle about a short-term place to live if the rent fell through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wired, like before an exam you haven't studied for. I'd still be up for it, but I'd be lying if I said I wasn't scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. What happens to your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means what I'm good at, learning fast, becomes the only thing I can sell. I'd have to be ready to switch twice, maybe three times. The upside is that I won't be stuck. The downside is the loan won't care how nimble I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about your housemates, the loan, the rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The three of us would stay together and pool cooking and bills to keep the rent down. We'd probably make a group chat for any job lead. The loan I can't do much about, except pay what I can and ask the lender for a break if work dries up.

say: I'd say it's not a **normal restructure** and the rules will have to change.
I'd say the firms making the savings should **pay** for the change.
think: I'd be lucky for **a year** or so, then the tools get better than me.
Using AI daily isn't a **moat** when the AI can do my job without me.
do: Cut costs to the bone and try to bank **500** a month with extra freelance.
Look for work built on **trust** and presence, like a local credit union.
Ask my uncle about a short-term **place to live** if rent fails.
feel: **Wired**, like before an exam I haven't studied for.
S2.quote: Using AI every day isn't a moat when the AI can do my job without me.
fieldNote: He admits his AI skill is **not** a moat once AGI is better than he is.
His plan is to keep switching; he expects to move more than once.
Group chat and pooled bills with housemates are his real safety net.

steps.text: Cut costs and bank 500 a month with extra freelance work
Look for roles at a credit union built on trust
Pool cooking and bills with my three housemates
Ask my uncle about a spare room if rent fails

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to build something if you start now. I'd talk about it as a chance, not just a threat, and I'd say people should learn the tools as soon as possible. I'd still push for a proper safety net, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think five years is the sweet spot for me: enough time to pay down part of the loan and build a small business or move into a role that's hard to automate. The risk is that I treat the time as a gift and waste it chasing too many ideas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the data and SQL courses, then build a small service for local businesses that sets up AI reporting and keeps it running. I'd aim to have five regular clients by the end of year two. I'd put 150 a month into paying down the loan and 50 into a rainy-day fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, with a nervous stomach. It feels like a race I can win only if I don't trip over the first hurdle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do with three more years than the fast version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build a bookkeeping-and-reporting service for independent shops, restaurants and small logistics firms. They can't afford a finance team but they can afford something I run on top of AI. It's work where trust matters, and being local helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you build?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can easily see the first year going well and the second year being a mess when a client leaves and I haven't saved enough. That's why the rainy-day fund isn't optional. I'd rather be boring about cash and bold about everything else.

say: I'd say five years is long enough to **build** something if you start now.
I'd still push for a proper **safety net**.
think: Five years is the **sweet spot** to pay down some loan and build something hard to automate.
My risk is treating the time as a gift and **chasing** too many ideas.
do: Finish the data and **SQL** courses, then launch a small AI-reporting service.
Aim for **five** regular clients by the end of year two.
Put **150** a month on the loan and 50 in a rainy-day fund.
feel: **Excited** with a nervous stomach, like a race I can win if I don't trip.
S3.quote: I'd rather be boring about cash and bold about everything else.
fieldNote: Five years turns his adaptability into a concrete **business** plan.
He names his own weakness: too many ideas and too little cash buffer.
He keeps a safety-net politics view even while building his own route.

steps.text: Finish the data and SQL courses
Launch an AI reporting service for small local shops
Put 150 a month on the loan and 50 in rainy-day savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the best case, because there's time to prepare, so we've no excuse. I'd say schools and employers should teach people how to work with the tools now, and that governments should plan for a bigger shift later. I'd be pretty chilled about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be calm. By 2036 I'd be 32 and could have a small business and a paid-off loan. The danger is that ten years sounds like forever, and then it's gone. People will keep waiting for a sign and the sign comes too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build my service business steadily, get the loan cleared in about six years, and look at moving into a product role at a finance technology firm. I'd put money into an index fund and keep learning every new tool as it appears. I'd also volunteer at a local school's careers day to talk about these tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good. Not carefree, because the loan is still a weight, but I feel like I'd have a say in how it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Is there any danger in having so long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The danger is drifting. If I do well in the first five years I'd feel safe, and that's exactly when the ground moves. I'd put a reminder in my calendar every January to ask what I'd do if my work disappeared in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell people younger than you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people younger than me to get curious early. Pick a skill that involves people, and don't take on a big loan for a degree without asking what it leads to. It's not complicated advice, but I wish somebody had pushed it on me at 17.

say: I'd say it's the **best case**, so there's no excuse not to prepare.
I'd say schools should teach people to work with the tools **now**.
think: By 2036 I'd be 32 with a small business and a **paid-off** loan.
Ten years sounds like forever, then it's **gone**, because the sign comes too late.
do: Build my service business steadily and **clear** the loan in about six years.
Look at a **product role** at a finance technology firm.
Put a small amount monthly in an **index fund**.
feel: Pretty **good**, though the loan is still a weight.
S4.quote: Pick a skill that involves people, and don't take on a big loan for a degree without asking what it leads to.
fieldNote: Ten years is the only scenario where he sounds truly **calm**.
He worries about drifting, and plans a yearly check-in with himself.
His advice to younger people comes from regret about his own loan.

steps.text: Grow my reporting service steadily and clear the loan in six years
Put a small amount monthly in an index fund
Keep learning each new AI tool as it appears

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'm fast on my feet, but a loan doesn't care how fast you are, and with two years I'd have no cushion at all. What would help is money to fall back on while I switch, something like a retraining grant or income support, and employers who share the savings instead of keeping them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me are called lucky because we know the tools, but luck runs out. I'd like the people who run the economy to plan for the version of me who isn't so lucky.

headlineQuote: People like me are called lucky because we know the tools, but luck runs out.
portrait: Carlos is a **22-year-old** junior finance analyst near Birmingham who uses AI every day and freelances for small firms on the side.
He's progressive and wants firms and governments to share the savings, while he moves fast to ride the change himself.
He carries a huge student loan and almost no savings, and that, not the technology, is what makes him uneasy.
His mood stays uneasy through most worlds, turns anxious only when AGI arrives in two years, and is calm with ten.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because his loan and thin cushion leave no room to switch work twice.
whatWouldHelp: Income **support** or a retraining grant while he switches, and employers who share the savings.
